papers.title: Spatial variation and correlates of raised blood pressure in Cambodia: a Gaussian-process geostatistical analysis of the 2023 STEPwise survey
papers.abstract: Introduction: Raised blood pressure is an important cardiovascular risk factor in Cambodia; however, national averages may obscure substantial local geographic heterogeneity. We assessed the spatial distribution of raised blood pressure and its demographic, metabolic, behavioural, built-environment, and environmental correlates using the 2023 Cambodia STEPwise approach to noncommunicable disease (NCD) risk factor surveillance (STEPS) survey. Methods: We analysed 289 georeferenced primary sampling units (PSUs) from the 2023 Cambodia STEPS Survey. PSU-level case counts and numbers of adults with valid blood pressure data were modelled using a frequentist binomial generalised additive model with a two-dimensional Gaussian-process smooth. An explanatory model included selected PSU-level and contextual covariates; a separate mapping model used spatially continuous predictors to generate predictions on a 5-km grid. Design-based national and residence-specific prevalence estimates were calculated separately using the survey design and Step-2 weights. Results: Among 4,225 adults with valid blood pressure data, unweighted prevalence of raised blood pressure was 28.6%, compared with 18.8% after Step-2 weighting; weighted prevalence was 17.5% in rural areas and 21.7% in urban/suburban areas. Mean observed unweighted PSU-level prevalence was 29.0%. In the adjusted spatial explanatory model, the proportion aged 60-69 years ({beta}=1.969, SE=0.327; p<0.001) and overweight/obesity prevalence ({beta}=0.996, SE=0.265; p<0.001) were positive ecological correlates. The spatial model had lower Akaike information criterion and residual deviance than its non-spatial counterpart, although Bayesian information criterion was higher. Prediction uncertainty was greater in some sparsely sampled areas. Conclusions: Raised blood pressure showed significant geographic heterogeneity across Cambodia. Older age composition and overweight/obesity prevalence were positive PSU-level correlates, not individual-level causal effects. Predicted prevalence should be interpreted alongside uncertainty and should complement, rather than replace, design-based STEPS prevalence estimates for geographically informed NCD planning.

papers.title: Beyond Usual Pace: Quick Walking Speed and Brain Health Outcomes in the Framingham Heart Study
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Stroke, dementia, and late-life depression share overlapping vascular pathophysiology, yet simple markers of shared neurological vulnerability across these conditions remain limited. Most gait research has relied on usual walking speed (UWS) alone, leaving it unclear whether quick walking speed (QWS) and gait adaptability (QWS minus UWS), relate to these conditions in the same way. METHODS: We examined associations of UWS, QWS, and gait adaptability with executive function, verbal memory, depressive symptoms, and incident stroke and dementia in the Framingham Heart Study Offspring cohort. A larger sample (n=2,308; mean age 61.5 years [SD 9.2]; 54% women) was used for cross-sectional and stroke analyses, and a dementia-free sample of 1,148 participants aged 60 years or older (mean age 68.5 years [SD 5.8]; 53% women) was used for analyses of incident dementia. We estimated associations per SD slower walking or smaller adaptability using linear, logistic, and Cox regression (10-year follow-up), overall and in women and men. RESULTS: Slower QWS and UWS were each associated with worse executive function, higher odds of high depressive symptoms (QWS OR 1.24, 95% CI 1.07-1.45; UWS OR 1.26, 95% CI 1.09-1.46), and greater hazard of incident stroke (QWS HR 1.30, 95% CI 1.03-1.64; UWS HR 1.36, 95% CI 1.11-1.65). Executive function and stroke associations were observed primarily in men (stroke QWS HR 1.55, 95% CI 1.11-2.17). For incident dementia, slower QWS reached significance (HR 1.34, 95% CI 1.10-1.63), while UWS did not (HR 1.20, 95% CI 0.98-1.46). Lower gait adaptability was associated with worse executive function overall and in women and men, and with incident dementia in women (HR 1.35, 95% CI 1.04-1.76), but not with depressive symptoms or stroke. No gait measure was associated with delayed recall. CONCLUSION: Slower QWS was associated with incident dementia; UWS was not. Adding a brief quick walking trial to routine gait assessment may identify risk that habitual-pace screening overlooks.

papers.title: Enhancing Scientific Validity by Integrating EHR and Claims Data in the National Clinical Cohort Collaborative
papers.abstract: Purpose: Accurately capturing a patient's health journey is essential for ensuring the validity of scientific and public health studies. Electronic health records (EHR) and administrative claims are commonly used in healthcare research, albeit separately. Previous research has demonstrated that EHR and claims capture different aspects of patient history and care, potentially introducing bias when used alone. In this study, we leveraged the largest public US EHR resource, the National Clinical Cohort Collaborative (N3C), alongside Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) claims data to compare their information coverage and agreement. Methods: We integrated N3C EHR and CMS data to create one cohesive dataset and quantified the proportion of key variables present in EHR alone, CMS alone, and the overlap present in both data sources. Overlap in information coverage was quantified pre- and post-landmark diagnosis of COVID-19. To evaluate the impact of data coverage differences, we conducted a case study evaluating the effect of COVID-19 vaccination on ischemic stroke using both data sources alone and in combination. Results: CMS data helped identify many individuals that were duplicated among EHR identifiers. Examination of the overlap showed that CMS data more completely captured conditions, while EHR data more completely captured medications after COVID-19 diagnosis. Some variables exhibited marked differences over time after landmark COVID-19 diagnosis. Using target trial emulation and self-controlled case series methods, we found that data capture variations altered effect estimates: EHR data alone yielded lower risk of ischemic stroke after vaccination in the target trial emulation (odds ratio 0.47, 95% CI 0.28-0.79), with a smaller, non-significant reduction in the self-controlled case series (incidence rate ratio 0.81, 95% CI 0.64-1.02), whereas analyses using CMS data alone or both sources combined yielded estimates close to the null in both designs. Conclusions: Results indicated that when using either a national database combining multiple EHR sources, or CMS claims data alone, patients' medical histories are less completely captured compared to when these data sources are combined. Case study results highlighted the value of combining data sources for not only yielding fuller patient health histories and valid scientific results, but for identifying and explaining biases that may emerge in research studies that rely on a single data source.

papers.title: Physical Activity Initiation and Incident Mobility Difficulty Among Older Adults: A Sequential Target Trial Emulation
papers.abstract: Although physical activity is associated with better physical functioning, the effects of initiating regular physical activity among older adults with persistent inactivity remain unclear. We conducted a sequential target trial emulation using Health and Retirement Study (HRS) data to estimate the effect of physical activity initiation versus noninitiation on incident mobility difficulty. Participants were included in the analysis if they were aged [≥]65 years at the previous wave, reported no regular physical activity at the previous two waves, and had no mobility, activities of daily living (ADL), or instrumental activities of daily living (IADL) difficulties at baseline. Stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting was applied to adjust for measured confounding. Weighted cumulative incidence was then estimated with death treated as a competing event, and risk differences were calculated at approximately 2, 4, and 6 years. At 2 years, the cumulative incidence of mobility difficulty was 32.75% among initiators and 39.73% among noninitiators, with a risk difference of -6.98 percentage points (95% CI, -13.11 to -0.88). At 4 and 6 years, risk differences were -2.90 percentage points (95% CI, -9.77 to 4.29) and -5.44 percentage points (95% CI, -12.27 to 1.99), respectively. Initiating regular moderate or vigorous physical activity was associated with a lower risk of incident mobility difficulty at approximately 2 years among older adults with persistent inactivity. This difference was less evident at later follow-up, and no clear differences were observed for incident ADL or IADL difficulty.

papers.title: Intersectional Trajectories in Physical and Mental Health: A UK Longitudinal Study (2009-2024)
papers.abstract: Health inequalities are often examined through single axes such as class or ethnicity, obscuring how these dimensions interlock. This study applies a longitudinal intersectional approach to examine physical and mental health trajectories across five generations in the UK. We analysed 14 waves of the UK Household Longitudinal Study (2009-2024) using longitudinal Multilevel Analysis of Individual Heterogeneity and Discriminatory Accuracy (MAIHDA). We modelled SF-12 physical and mental health trajectories for 398 intersectional strata defined by gender, ethnicity, occupational class, and generation. Physical health inequalities widened with age, consistent with cumulative disadvantage, while mental health inequalities were more evident among later-born cohorts. The 'Boomer' generation exhibited a relatively flat mental health trajectory across its observed age range. In contrast, 'Generation Z' had lower predicted mental health, particularly among White British women with no work history - a group with poorer predicted trajectories than their South Asian peers. Our study shows how health inequalities are structurally differentiated by cohort and intersectional position. Policy responses should support proportionate universalism, combining broad population-level support with intensified action for groups showing poorer health.

papers.title: Accuracy and completeness of death recording in primary care electronic health records compared with national death registrations in England using OpenSAFELY-TPP
papers.abstract: Introduction: Primary care electronic health records (EHRs) are an important resource for health research, but death recording in primary care EHRs may be incomplete or differ from Office for National Statistics (ONS) death registrations. We used OpenSAFELY-TPP to assess the completeness and concordance of death recording and provide recommendations for using date-of-death information. Methods: Using linked primary care EHRs and ONS death registrations, we assessed whether ONS-registered deaths from 2020-2025 had a primary care date of death and, where present, calculated the difference between dates. Where a primary care date was absent, we assessed death-related SNOMED CT codes. Analyses were conducted overall and by year, population subgroup, and general practice. We also examined GP registration end dates and primary-care-recorded deaths without a corresponding ONS record, including monthly patterns near the data extraction date. Results: Among 1,409,275 ONS-registered deaths, 88% had the same date recorded in primary care and 8% had no corresponding primary care date. Among 1,324,995 deaths recorded in primary care, <2% had no corresponding ONS record. Deaths recorded in only one source were more frequent among people aged <45 years and those from Mixed, Asian or Asian British, Black or Black British, and Chinese or Other ethnic groups. ONS-only dates were also more frequent in London and the West Midlands. Primary-care-only deaths increased close to date of data extraction, reaching 7% in February 2026. Same-day GP deregistration increased from 9% in 2020 to 85% in 2025. Conclusions: Death recording in primary care EHRs showed high completeness and concordance with ONS registrations, but discrepancies remained for recent deaths and some population groups. Data recency and population-specific completeness should therefore be considered when using linked mortality data for research.

papers.title: High-sensitivity C-reactive protein profiles differ between Korean and US adults with LDL cholesterol below 100 mg/dL
papers.abstract: Objectives: To compare high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP) profiles in Korean and US adults with low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) below 100 mg/dL and examine differences after adiposity adjustment. Study design: Cross-sectional analysis of national health examination surveys. Methods: We analysed the Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 2022-2024 (n=5,785) and US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey August 2021-August 2023 (n=1,056). Eligible adults had Sampson-calculated LDL-C below 100 mg/dL and hsCRP of 10 mg/L or less; elevated hsCRP was defined as 2-10 mg/L. We estimated survey-weighted prevalence differences and adjusted prevalence ratios (PRs). Results: LDL-C distributions closely overlapped (weighted medians, 79.7 vs 80.1 mg/dL), whereas median hsCRP was 0.50 vs 1.34 mg/L. Elevated-hsCRP prevalence was 12.2% in Korea and 35.7% in the United States (difference, 23.5 percentage points; 95% CI, 19.4-27.7); the age-sex-standardised difference was 23.4 percentage points. Among 6,235 common complete cases, the age-sex-adjusted US-versus-Korea PR was 2.86 (95% CI, 2.48-3.30), decreasing to 1.66 (1.40-1.98) after waist circumference adjustment and 1.92 (1.62-2.26) after body mass index adjustment. Conclusions: Similar LDL-C distributions coexisted with markedly different hsCRP profiles. Waist adjustment attenuated the between-country contrast more than BMI adjustment, supporting joint consideration of inflammatory, lipid and anthropometric measures in population surveillance.

papers.title: Systemic and organ-specific proteomic aging clocks as predictors of cancer incidence and survival: insights from the Finnish Twin Cohort
papers.abstract: Despite recent evidence of the ability of systemic and organ-specific proteomic aging clocks to predict a large range of age-related diseases, their utility in cancer research remains largely underexplored. In this study, we evaluated the predictive ability of systemic and organ-specific proteomic aging clocks for (i) all-cause mortality, (ii) cancer-related mortality, and (iii) cancer incidence in a sample of Finnish twins (N = 401, mean age at baseline 62.3 years) with Olink proteomic data. Participants were followed for a mean of 10.6 years (SD +- 1.6), with estimates from four systemic and 18 organ-specific proteomic aging clocks calculated at baseline. Cox proportional hazards regression models adjusted for sex and age at baseline identified 15 proteomic aging clocks as significant predictors of all-cause mortality (Ncases = 28) after multiple testing correction (FDR < 0.05), with 11 remaining significant after lifestyle adjustment (Ncases = 27). For several clocks, effect sizes were large, with hazard ratios (HR) approximately doubling per one standard deviation (SD) increase in clock estimates. In predicting cancer-related deaths among participants without a prior cancer diagnosis at baseline (Ncases = 9), only the Immune clock showed a significant positive association after multiple testing correction in basic (HR = 2.94, 95% CI: 1.88-4.59) and lifestyle-adjusted models (HR = 3.31, 95% CI: 1.78-6.17). No associations with cancer incidence (Ncases = 34 basic, Ncases = 31 adjusted) survived multiple testing correction, although several nominal associations were observed. In conclusion, our findings suggest that proteomic aging clocks are strong predictors of all-cause and cancer-specific mortality, independent of lifestyle factors. Proteomic aging clocks may further serve as valuable tools for stratifying cancers by mortality risk.

papers.title: TrialCalibre1: An Agentic System for Trial Emulation, Benchmarking, and Calibration
papers.abstract: TrialCalibre1 is an agentic system that connects clinical evidence, study design, and executable analyses. It supports reference-trial replication, direct target-trial emulation, and BenchExCal, which combines benchmarking, extension, and cal ibration sensitivity analysis. We evaluated an ASCET-based benchmark and an extension comparing clopidogrel with aspirin among adults aged 81-90 years us ing synthetic PCORnet-style claims. Two reviewers assessed benchmark extrac tion, protocol decisions, and implementation. After discussion, 53/62 and 50/62 assessable SQL checks were rated met; both reviewers rated 12/13 assessable R checks met. Protocol and proxy disagreements remained. A separate ten-question routing development set yielded 10/10 route matches and 7/7 applicable reference trial matches. The agent benchmark and extension included 6,069 and 1,602 pa tients. The extension risk ratio was 0.848 (95% CI 0.569-1.184), with a calibrated sensitivity estimate of 1.274 (0.439-3.700). The human implementation provided descriptive comparisons, not same-data validation. Dose proxies, unpopulated co variates, residual imbalance, implementation deviations, and ignored cross-cohort covariance limited interpretation. This case demonstrates a connected workflow whose protocols, code, and results can be reviewed.

papers.title: Whole person health across sociodemographic groups of adults in the United States
papers.abstract: Chronic disease accounts for most health care expenditures in the United States (US), highlighting the need for approaches that address health across interconnected spiritual, mental/emotional, behavioral, physical (including environmental), and social domains. Whole person health (WPH) is increasingly recognized as important for alleviating chronic disease burdens but has not been well-described across various sociodemographic groups of US adults. Using cross-sectional data from the 2025 National Health Interview Survey, we sought to describe the prevalence of WPH and its components among US adults overall and by age, sex, and race along with ethnicity. Participants responded to the nine-item Whole Person Health Index (WPHI), which we used to assess continuous scores (range: 9-45, where higher scores indicated improved health) and ''optimal'' (excellent/very good vs. good/fair/poor) overall and domain-specific WPH. Using survey procedures, we estimated medians (IQR) and prevalence (95% CI) and compared subgroups using multiple comparison correction. Among 23,884 NHIS participants aged 18 years and older (mean age (SE)=48 (0.2) years), representing approximately 261,620,640 US adults, the median WPHI score was 33 (28-37) and slightly over half (57% [56%-58%]) of adults were classified as having ''optimal'' overall WPH. Optimal social/family connections (72% [72%-73%]) were frequently reported; ''optimal'' sleep was infrequently reported (36% [35%-37%]). WPH and its components were generally highest among younger adults. Men and women differed in WPH domains but not in overall WPH. Non-Hispanic (NH) American Indian/Native Alaskan and NH-Black adults generally had lowest prevalence of optimal WPH and its components, which was often higher among Hispanic/Latino adults and highest among NH-Asian and White adults. These results showing variation in WPH in the US may inform future investigations of WPH, related predictors and health outcomes, and health disparities.

papers.title: Testing structural interpretations beyond goodness-of-fit in a phenomenological epidemic model: A reproducibility-oriented case study
papers.abstract: Simulation models are widely used to support counterfactual inference in settings where direct experimental validation is difficult or infeasible. However, for phenomenological models calibrated to observational time series, goodness-of-fit does not necessarily establish that the structural assumptions underlying such inferences are uniquely supported by the data. Here, we examine this issue using a published COVID-19 transmission model for Japan that incorporates empirical inputs including human mobility, variant prevalence, and vaccination and has been used to estimate the effects of alternative vaccination scenarios. Using the publicly archived code together with a reconstructed substitute for a restricted-access input file required by the released implementation, we first reproduced the published model behaviour. We then performed two complementary computational stress tests. First, the vaccination-related input was suppressed and the remaining parameters were re-estimated against the original epidemic trajectory. Second, as a complementary test of trajectory-level flexibility, the model was refitted to synthetic target series with qualitatively different temporal structures while retaining the empirical mobility and variant inputs. The model retained substantial fitting capacity in both tests: suppression of the vaccination-related input caused only a limited deterioration in fit to the original trajectory, while qualitatively different synthetic trajectories could also be reproduced through parameter adjustment. Variation in fitted parameters across these conditions was also consistent with compensatory parameter behaviour. These results do not imply that vaccination had no effect or that the original model is invalid. Rather, they provide empirical evidence that, in this case, goodness-of-fit to the observed epidemic trajectory alone does not uniquely support the structural interpretation required for vaccination-related counterfactual inference. The study illustrates the value of reproducible computational stress testing as a complement to, rather than a substitute for, formal identifiability or model-comparison analyses.

papers.title: Approach to some data preparation problems in systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.abstract: In systematic review, the measures reported by the primary studies may not always be the measures sought by the systematic review investigators. Motivated by an systematic review of interventions to reduce meat consumption, we discuss here methods to infer relative risks and confidence intervals from randomized controlled trials that reported differences, possibly in the presence of repeated measures or multiple interventions.

papers.title: Development and Validation of a Sleep Disorder Risk Prediction Model in Young and Middle-Aged Adults With Anemia
papers.abstract: ObjectiveThis study aimed to develop and validate a predictive model for sleep disorders in young and middle-aged adults with anemia, providing evidence for early identification, risk stratification, and individualized sleep management. MethodsData in the NHANES were analyzed and randomly divided into development and validation cohorts. LASSO regression was used to screen optimal predictors in the development cohort, followed by univariate and multivariate logistic regression to identify independent predictors and construct a nomogram. Model performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic curves, calibration curves, Brier scores, and decision curve analysis. ResultsThe weighted prevalence of sleep disorders among young and middle-aged adults with anemia was 10.19%. Multivariate logistic regression identified seven independent predictors: sex, monocyte count, asthma, overweight, arthritis, congestive heart failure, and hypertension. The model showed good discrimination, with area under the curve values of 0.817 in the development cohort and 0.791 in the validation cohort. Calibration was satisfactory, with Brier scores of 0.074 and 0.075, respectively. Decision curve analysis indicated favorable clinical net benefit in both cohorts. ConclusionThe proposed predictive model demonstrated good discrimination, calibration, and may help healthcare providers identify young and middle-aged adults with anemia who are at high risk for sleep disorders.

papers.title: Patterns and correlates of alcohol and other substance use among adults in two communities in Cape Town: a cross-sectional
papers.abstract: BackgroundWe aimed to characterize substance use patterns, and their correlates, among adults with and without HIV at two healthcare facilities in Cape Town, South Africa. MethodsWe recruited adults with and without HIV from two primary healthcare facilities. We assessed alcohol use with the AUDIT-C and other substance use with the WHO-ASSIST questionnaires. We classified participants with no lifetime drug use and no or low-risk alcohol use as "low risk" and fitted latent class models among remaining participants to identify additional substance use patterns. We used multinomial logistic regression to examine factors associated with substance use patterns. ResultsAmong 602 participants, 265 (44.0%) were "low risk". Latent class analysis among the remaining 337 identified three patterns: "higher-risk alcohol use" (N=168; 27.9%), "cannabis use" (universal cannabis use with mixed alcohol risk; N=114; 18.9%), and "mixed illicit drug use" (predominantly no or low-risk alcohol use with use of multiple drugs; N=55; 9.1%). Participants younger than 45 years were less likely to be in the low-risk group. Male sex was associated with lower probability of the low-risk group and higher probability of the higher-risk alcohol use and cannabis use classes. HIV was associated with higher probability of higher-risk alcohol use. One facility had a substantially higher probability of mixed illicit drug use. ConclusionsWe identified distinct higher-risk substance use profiles that varied strongly by age, sex, and facility. These findings support integrating alcohol and substance use screening and management into primary care and tailoring responses to local substance use patterns.

papers.title: Visit-to-Visit Blood Pressure Variability, Glycemic Status and the Risk of Dementia, Stroke, and All-Cause Mortality: A UK Biobank Cohort Study
papers.abstract: Aims: The risks of dementia, stroke, and mortality increase from normoglycemia to prediabetes and type 2 diabetes (T2D). Blood pressure variability (BPV) is associated with adverse vascular and neurological outcomes, but its role in glycemia-associated risks remains unclear. We examined the interplay between glycemia, BPV, and these outcomes. Methods and Results: In a large prospective cohort, visit-to-visit BPV was quantified using absolute and directional measures of systolic (SBP), diastolic (DBP), mean arterial (MAP), and pulse pressure (PP). Glycemic status was defined as normoglycemia, prediabetes, and T2D. Time-updated Cox models estimated outcome associations, adjusting for confounders and mean blood pressure. We evaluated the joint and independent associations of BPV and glycemic status with outcomes, effect modification, and attenuation of glycemia-associated risks after BPV adjustment. Among 57,611 participants (median follow-up, 5.1 years; IQR, 3.3-9.5 years), compared with normoglycemia and low BPV, T2D with high SBP variability was associated with higher risks of all-cause mortality (HR 2.80, 95% CI 2.12-3.69) and nominally higher risk of all-cause dementia (HR 2.46, 95% CI 1.37-4.42). All absolute BPV measures were independently associated with mortality, while DBP and MAP variability were associated with overall stroke after FDR correction. Additional adjustment for BPV minimally attenuated glycemia-associated risk, and no multiplicative interaction remained significant after multiple-testing correction. Conclusions: Absolute BPV was associated with mortality, and DBP and MAP variability with overall stroke, after accounting for glycemic status and mean blood pressure. Additional BPV adjustment changed the glycemic association only minimally.

papers.title: Language eligibility criteria and enrolled racial and ethnic composition in US clinical trials: a cross-sectional study
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Federal policy now requires sponsors to submit diversity action plans for clinical trials, yet the modifiable features of trial design associated with enrolled composition remain poorly characterized. English-language proficiency requirements are written into eligibility criteria and recorded as free text in a public registry, making them visible and, in principle, amenable to revision, but their relationship to enrolled composition has been examined only within single disease areas and in small samples of trials. We examined whether these requirements and documented language accommodation were associated with the racial and ethnic composition of enrolled participants. METHODS AND FINDINGS: We conducted a cross-sectional study of interventional trials registered on ClinicalTrials.gov with at least one US site and posted results, using a registry snapshot retrieved in October 2026. The primary cohort comprised the 44,487 trials with exclusively US sites, of which 21,924 (49.3%) reported baseline race and 17,434 (39.2%) reported baseline ethnicity with counts that reconciled with the posted denominator. Both exposures were classified from free-text eligibility criteria using regular expressions validated against independent physician review of 150 trials. For the English-language requirement classifier, sensitivity was 88.2% and specificity was 99.2%. The outcome was the trial-level proportion of enrolled participants in each category, analyzed using generalized linear models adjusted for intervention class, therapeutic area, sponsor, phase, enrollment, sites, start year, US Census region, and the population composition of the trial's site states. An English-language proficiency requirement appeared in 5,736 trials (12.9%); its prevalence rose from 7.4% of trials starting in 2010 to 26.2% in 2023 (odds ratio [OR] per decade 2.91, P<0.001), whereas documented accommodation, an eligibility statement allowing participation in a language other than English (Spanish in 99.9% of flagged trials), remained rare (788 trials, 1.8%). The requirement was associated with lower enrolled proportions of Asian (OR=0.85, 95% CI 0.77-0.93, P=0.001) and Hispanic/Latinx participants (OR=0.85, 95% CI 0.79-0.91, P<0.001), with no evidence of an association for White participants (OR=0.99, 95% CI 0.95-1.04, P=0.75). Documented accommodation was associated with a higher proportion of Hispanic/Latinx participants (OR=3.23, 95% CI 2.82-3.71, P<0.001). Geographic adjustment did not change the statistical significance of the requirement associations and attenuated the accommodation association. The main limitations were the cross-sectional design, which precludes causal inference; the restriction of enrollment analyses to trials reporting baseline demographics, which were more recent than those without such reporting; and possible misclassification of automatically classified exposures. CONCLUSIONS: English-language proficiency requirements became more than three times as common between 2010 and 2023 and were associated with lower enrolled proportions of Asian and Hispanic/Latinx participants. Less common documented language accommodation was associated with a higher enrolled proportion of Hispanic/Latinx participants. Because these criteria are investigator-written and publicly recorded, they may be a tractable target for improving enrollment equity, although whether revising them changes who enrolls requires prospective evaluation

papers.title: Dynamics of a slow-burn epidemic: the genomic epidemiology of poultry-associated Campylobacter jejuni ST474 in New Zealand
papers.abstract: The emergence of a dominant poultry-associated strain of Campylobacter jejuni in New Zealand coincided with a multi-year epidemic of human campylobacteriosis. This was characterised by an increase in cases to 2006, when one of the highest national case-rates in the world was recorded, followed by a rapid decline attributed to interventions in the poultry industry. The strain belonged to an internationally rare multilocus sequence type, ST474 - a member of Clonal Complex (CC) 48 - that was highly prevalent in both poultry and human cases in New Zealand but was also identified in other samples. ST474 isolates from humans, animal reservoirs and environmental water samples were collected between 2005 and 2019 and whole genome sequenced (N=443). Isolates from a 2018/9 case-control study of campylobacteriosis in New Zealand were included for genomic comparisons with other sequence types and CCs. This presented an opportunity to examine the genomic epidemiology of a single, relatively recently emerged lineage of C. jejuni, and improve our understanding of drivers of emergence and persistence in a relatively isolated ecosystem. Six subpopulations (clades) of ST474 were identified and these varied in terms of their host association, persistence, patterns of homologous recombination, and complement of mobile genetic elements, including plasmids and chromosomally integrated elements. Clade E was associated with a single poultry supplier in the initial epidemic phase and accounted for 34.5% of human cases. Clade F emerged from a declining Clade E after the peak in human cases and was also associated with poultry. The emergence of Clade F was accompanied by the loss of integrated element CJIE5 and the acquisition of multiple blocks of recombination, likely from diverse ancestral C. jejuni lineages, and the loss of the methionine biosynthesis operon metAB. In contrast, Clades A-D were detected at low frequencies in human cases over the 14-year period of surveillance and were associated with multiple hosts. This longitudinal study sheds light on the evolutionary processes that result in strain emergence and differentiation, highlighting the role of horizontal gene transfer in the evolution and adaptation of this pathogen to new niches, and the subsequent impact on public health.

papers.title: EpiAlert: A Transparent CUSUM-EWMA Framework for Early Warning of Unusual Influenza-Like Illness Surveillance Activity
papers.abstract: Automated surveillance systems can prove to be extremely useful in detecting outbreaks of respiratory diseases that need further epidemiological investigation. In order for the system to be effective, careful attention has to be paid to the baseline used, absence of the observations, and the use of proper statistical methods. As a solution, the paper describes EpiAlert, a weekly surveillance system based on CDC FluView ILINet. The system is able to transform the number of ILI visits and the total number of visits into a ILI prevalence for the region, create the first reference from the three previous years using a +/-2-week interval, transform the rate value, and apply two different detectors - CUSUM and EWMA. CUSUM is set at k=0.5 and h=5, whereas EWMA uses {lambda}=0.2 and H=2.7 values. Among the 55 districts, the system gives 45,138 pieces of information about the disease by transforming 44,297 pieces of data into alerts. It is found that there are 2,820 alerts in total (out of which 2,711 alerts used CUSUM, 402 used EWMA, and 293 used both detectors). Additionally, the experiments show that the sensitivity of the device depends greatly on the detector. The latest statistics can be tracked in the report for week 37 of 2026 that recently concluded in West.

papers.title: Does handgrip strength improve cardiometabolic risk stratification beyond detailed body composition? NHANES 2011-2014 with temporal validation
papers.abstract: BackgroundHandgrip strength is associated with cardiometabolic abnormalities, but whether it adds information once detailed adiposity and muscle mass are known is unclear. MethodsWe studied adults aged 40-59 years from NHANES 2011-2012 (development, n=508) and 2013-2014 (temporal validation, n=616). The outcome was at least two of four non-adiposity abnormalities (elevated blood pressure, fasting glucose or triglycerides, or low HDL cholesterol); waist circumference was not part of the outcome. A prespecified feature ladder added DXA body fat percentage and visceral adipose tissue to age, sex, BMI and waist circumference (M1), then appendicular skeletal muscle index (M2), then absolute (M3A, primary) or weight-normalised (M3B) grip strength. Logistic regression was primary; elastic-net and XGBoost were supportive. Development performance used nested cross-validation; frozen models were scored once in the validation cohort. Paired increments used 2000 stratified bootstrap resamples. ResultsThe outcome occurred in 249 (49.0%) and 277 (45.0%) participants. Adding adiposity increased the logistic regression AUC by 0.0209 (95% CI 0.0024-0.0402) in development and 0.0209 (0.0032-0.0375) in temporal validation. Adding absolute grip strength to M2 changed the AUC by -0.0046 (-0.0107 to 0.0013) and 0.0045 (-0.0009 to 0.0098), respectively. All 12 grip-strength AUC increments across algorithms, definitions and cohorts had intervals that included zero. Calibration was unchanged and the incremental net benefit was not consistently positive. Model attributions to grip strength varied by algorithm. ConclusionsIn middle-aged adults, detailed adiposity, but not grip strength, added reproducible information for concurrent cardiometabolic risk stratification beyond conventional anthropometry and muscle mass. HighlightsO_LIDXA adiposity added about 0.02 AUC in both development and temporal validation C_LIO_LIGrip strength added no stable increment beyond adiposity and muscle mass C_LIO_LIAll 12 grip-strength AUC increments had 95% CIs that included zero C_LIO_LIGrip strength received model attributions that did not improve performance C_LIO_LIFrozen models were scored once in a later, temporally separated NHANES cycle C_LI

papers.title: A Novel Digital Phenotype of Physical Activity: Associations with Heart Rate Fragmentation
papers.abstract: BackgroundHeart rate fragmentation (HRF) has emerged as a novel marker of sinoatrial instability and neuroautonomic dysregulation and is a predictor of incident cardiovascular disease (CVD) events and cardiovascular mortality. Leveraging heart rate fragmentation as a novel measure may help us better understand the prognostic significance of physical activity. Physical activity (PA) patterns are multidimensional and difficult to study holistically, however. We sought to examine for novel PA clusters in a cohort of veteran men and evaluate their prognostic significance based on their associations with neuroautonomic dysregulation. MethodsIn this cross-sectional study, we examined 602 male veterans from the Vietnam Era Twins Study of Electrophysiology in Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (VETS-EP) who were enrolled between 2022 and 2026. Accelerometry data were used to derive physical activity parameters across 6 domains: volume, sedentary behavior, intensity, diurnal pattern, fragmentation, and variability. Heart rate fragmentation was assessed using percentage of inflection points (PIP), inverse average length of segments (IALS), percentage of short segments (PSS), and percentage of alternating segments (PAS). Gaussian mixture models were used to derive digital phenotypes of physical activity, and associations with heart rate fragmentation were assessed using linear mixed models. ResultsParticipants had a mean age of 73.8 {+/-} 2.9 years and 93.2% reported White race. Two overlapping phenotypes of physical activity patterns were identified: a compact-early phenotype, characterized by earlier activity timing and slightly greater overall activity, and a diffuse-late phenotype, characterized by later activity timing and greater heterogeneity in activity volume. In fully adjusted models, the diffuse-late phenotype was associated with higher PIP, the primary outcome ({beta}: 1.199, 95% CI: 0.034 to 2.363, p-value: 0.044), and higher IALS ({beta}: 0.01210, 95% CI: 0.00048 to 0.02373, p-value: 0.041), but not PSS or PAS, compared with the compact-early phenotype. ConclusionsIn older male veterans, Gaussian mixture model phenotyping identified two overlapping physical activity phenotypes, differing mainly in diurnal timing and in the dispersion of overall activity, that were associated with modest differences in heart rate fragmentation. These phenotypes provide a framework for capturing complex physical activity patterns. Future prospective studies representing diverse populations are needed to validate such phenotypes.

papers.title: Mortality among Brazilian male police officers and firefighters over three decades
papers.abstract: BackgroundLong-term mortality data among Brazilian police officers and firefighters are scarce. This study investigated the leading causes of death in Brazilian male military police officers and firefighters over three decades, comparing their mortality and mean age at death with those of the male population. MethodsWe retrospectively analyzed death records of male military police officers and firefighters from Espirito Santo (ES), Brazil, from 1988 to 2019. Mortality was analyzed across three decades and the standardized mortality ratios (SMRs) for the three leading causes were calculated using the male populations of ES and Brazil as references. ResultsOverall, 2,198 deaths were identified, with a mean age at death of 59 {+/-} 18.5 years, compared with 60.5 {+/-} 23.9 years among men in ES and 63.4 {+/-} 23.7 years among Brazilian men. Mean age at death was 36 {+/-} 9 years among active-duty and 68 {+/-} 13 years among inactive personnel. Across the study population, the leading causes of death were circulatory system diseases (32%), external causes (26%) and neoplasms (15%). Circulatory disease mortality was higher in the second and third decades compared with both reference populations, whereas external-cause mortality shifted from higher, in the first two decades, to lower than expected in the last decade. Neoplasm mortality was higher relative to Brazil only in the last decade. ConclusionMortality patterns differed by cause and over time. The younger mean age at death among active-duty personnel, together with cause-specific excess mortality, highlights the importance of long-term occupational health surveillance and preventive strategies.

papers.title: Integrating Longitudinal Cohorts for Population Health Research: Mainland and Island-based Puerto Rican Diabetes Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundPopulation research increasingly relies on integrating data across studies to understand patterns of health and disease at broader scales. Such integration expands sample size and supports multimodal analyses, but independent cohort studies are often not directly comparable due to differences in instruments, timing, and measurement structure. Data harmonization addresses this challenge by transforming heterogeneous variables into comparable measures, allowing datasets collected under different protocols to be analyzed jointly, but published harmonization efforts seldom include an analysis conducted on the integrated dataset itself. MethodsWe developed an integrated dataset, combining two longitudinal cohorts, the Boston Puerto Rican Health Study (BPRHS) and the Puerto Rico Observational Study of Psychosocial, Environmental, and Chronic Disease Trends (PROSPECT). Comparability between variables was established through an explicit framework distinguishing availability from construct comparability, and the evidence supporting comparability is reported by class of feature, including tests of measurement invariance and differential test functioning for the multi-item psychosocial scales. To support transparency and reuse, we provide an open-source Python pipeline and structured metadata describing variable alignment and transformations. As a worked example of downstream use, we conducted a Random Forest analysis predicting diabetes status. ResultsThe integrated dataset comprises 539 harmonized variables across four BPRHS visits and two PROSPECT visits, each documented with its source variable, question wording, and transformation. In the worked example, the integrated dataset retained predictive signal relative to cohort-specific models and improved performance for the smaller cohort. ConclusionsThese findings illustrate how transparent, documented cross-cohort integration can support predictive population health research while making the basis for comparability explicit.

papers.title: Longitudinal personal environmental exposure and Streptococcus pneumoniae colonisation in a cohort of children 5-14 years old in rural Gambia.
papers.abstract: BackgroundAir pollution contributes substantially to morbidity and mortality in low-income countries, where reliance on solid fuels leads to high levels of household exposure. Colonisation of the upper respiratory tract by Streptococcus pneumoniae is a prerequisite for pneumococcal disease, and inhaled air pollutants may influence colonisation through impaired mucociliary clearance. Therefore, we investigated the association between S. pneumoniae colonisation and personal exposure to particulate matter (PM2.5) and carbon monoxide (CO) as well as temperature and relative humidity in older children in The Gambia. MethodsWe conducted a prospective study of 134 children aged 5-14 years across eight visits in rural Gambia. Personal 24-hour PM2.5, CO, temperature and relative humidity exposures were measured using personal monitors. Concurrently, combined nasopharyngeal/oropharyngeal swabs were collected at each visit, and S. pneumoniae colonisation was determined by microbiological culture. Mixed-effects logistic regression models were used to examine associations between environmental exposures and colonisation. Exposures were additionally decomposed into between-child and within-child components. Models were adjusted for age, season, and household income tertile. ResultsA total of 554 child visits with paired exposure and microbiological data were analysed. Overall, 24-hour geometric mean PM2.5 and CO were 12.6 {micro}g/m3 (95% CI 12.2-13.1) and 0.16 ppm (95% CI 0.14-0.19) respectively and overall S. pneumoniae colonisation prevalence was 39.7%. In conventional models, PM2.5, CO, temperature, and relative humidity were not significantly associated with S. pneumoniae colonisation after adjustment for confounders. In the within-between decomposition analysis, higher between-child temperature exposure was consistently associated with lower odds of colonisation (mutually adjusted model: OR 0.74, 95% CI 0.56-0.98; p = 0.034). Relative humidity showed an inverse within-child association in crude analysis (OR 0.70, 95% CI 0.52-0.93; p = 0.013), which attenuated after adjustment for season and other confounders. No associations were observed for PM2.5 or CO exposures. ConclusionAt the exposure levels observed in this cohort of older children, PM2.5 and CO exposures were not independently associated with S. pneumoniae colonisation. The pattern observed for temperature suggests that longer-term temperature conditions may be more relevant to pneumococcal colonisation than short-term exposure variation in this setting.

papers.title: Impact of Prolonged Obesity Across the Lifecourse on Myocardial Stress and Injury in Older Age: Birth Cohort Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe consequences of prolonged exposure to obesity on biomarkers of myocardial stress and injury remain unclear. We examined associations of duration and cumulative severity of obesity from childhood to later adulthood with concentrations of N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I (hs-cTnI), and growth differentiation factor-15 (GDF-15) at age 62 years. MethodsThe sample comprised 4,901 participants in the 1958 National Child Development Study who had measurements of NT-proBNP, hs-cTnI, or GDF-15 at age 62 years and at least four BMI assessments between 7 and 62 years of age. Individual BMI trajectories were modelled, from which total duration of obesity and mean excess BMI (area between the trajectory and the age-specific obesity threshold divided by duration) were derived. Associations of ever versus never having been obese, obesity duration, and mean excess BMI with biomarker concentrations were examined using general linear regression models with progressive adjustment for early-life characteristics; contemporaneous cardiometabolic factors; and health behaviours, socioeconomic position, and psychosocial factors. Nonlinear associations of obesity duration were estimated using restricted cubic splines and subsequently approximated using linear splines. ResultsOverall, 26.3% of participants had ever experienced obesity. There was no evidence of an association between ever versus never having been obese and NT-proBNP. Among men, ever having been obese was associated with 11.00% (95% CI, 4.62-17.37) higher hs-cTnI in the fully adjusted model, whereas there was no evidence of an association among women. Ever having been obese was associated with higher GDF-15, although the association attenuated substantially after adjustment for contemporaneous cardiometabolic factors. Longer obesity duration was associated with higher concentrations of all three biomarkers in fully adjusted models, but the pattern differed by biomarker: hs-cTnI increased approximately linearly with duration, whereas NT-proBNP and GDF-15 remained relatively stable up to approximately 25 years of obesity before increasing with longer duration. In fully adjusted models, each additional year of obesity beyond 25 years was associated with 1.80% (95% CI, 0.54-3.06) higher NT-proBNP and 0.81% (95% CI, 0.25-1.36) higher GDF-15, while each additional year across the full range of obesity duration was associated with 0.41% (95% CI, 0.07-0.76) higher hs-cTnI. Among participants who had ever experienced obesity, each 1 kg/m{superscript 2} higher mean excess BMI was associated with 4.02% (95% CI, 1.79-6.24) higher NT-proBNP and 2.00% (95% CI, 0.49-3.51) higher hs-cTnI in fully adjusted models; there was no evidence of an association with GDF-15. ConclusionsLonger duration of obesity was associated with higher concentrations of biomarkers reflecting myocardial stress, injury, and cellular stress at age 62 years, with associations particularly evident after approximately 25 years of obesity for NT-proBNP and GDF-15. These findings suggest that duration of obesity may provide clinically relevant information beyond current obesity status, supporting its consideration as an additional dimension of cumulative obesity burden in cardiovascular risk assessment.

papers.title: Quantifying Systematic Bias in Observational Causal Estimates Using Negative Controls: The Bias Attribution Fraction
papers.abstract: ImportanceObservational studies dominate evidence in cardiovascular outcomes research, yet no widely adopted reporting standard requires authors to disclose how much of an observed association is attributable to systematic error. The negative-control calibration framework of the Observational Health Data Sciences and Informatics consortium returns a binary answer: a calibrated P-value either crosses 0.05 or it does not. That answer conflates "is there a signal" with "is the signal credible." ObjectiveTo define the Bias Attribution Fraction (BAF), a continuous estimator in [0, 1] that quantifies the fraction of an observed log relative risk that is attributable to systematic bias, together with its 95% credible interval, and to evaluate whether reporting calibrated P-value plus BAF plus interval width produces more defensible decisions than reporting the calibrated P-value alone. DesignThree-part study: (i) metric definition and interval construction; (ii) Monte Carlo simulation across 1920 conditions x 1000 repetitions = 1,920,000 simulated target estimates (a primary grid plus a sign-flipped companion grid of identical size, pooled for all analyses), with truth known by construction; (iii) two-arm beta-blocker target trial emulation in MIMIC IV, adhering to the TARGET guideline, with targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) and 12 negative-control outcomes. SettingMIMIC IV (critical care) and MIMIC IV ECG, 2008 to 2019. ParticipantsAdults with a first intensive care unit stay and a recorded 12-lead ECG. ExposuresTwo clinical questions are evaluated: (1) reaching at least 50% of guideline-recommended target dose of an index beta-blocker within 7 days of admission, sustained to 12 months, versus lower or no exposure; (2) receiving guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) with at least two of three foundational drug classes at adequate dose for 12 months versus fewer. Main Outcomes and MeasuresOne-year all-cause mortality. Primary analytic outputs: (i) the calibrated P-value from a negative-control empirical null distribution with 12 outcomes; (ii) BA[F] with a Markov chain Monte Carlo 95% credible interval; (iii) a verdict drawn from a truth-calibrated lookup table mapping the BA[F] x interval-width cell to a probability of being bias-dominated. ResultsAcross 1,920,000 simulated repetitions, the calibrated P-value alone yielded a misuse rate (declared usable while truth was bias-dominated) of 36.02%. Adding the BAF point estimate reduced misuse to 16.48%, and requiring the whole credible interval of BAF to lie below 0.5, clear of the bias-dominated zone, reduced misuse to 10.16%. Requiring in addition a calibrated probability of bias dominance below 15% reduced misuse to 3.02% at the cost of declaring 22.1% of estimates usable (versus 61.8% for the calibrated P-value alone). Read from the bias-dominated view, meaning that withholding a repetition is a positive call and being truly bias-dominated is a positive truth, the BAF estimator achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.922, compared with 0.787 for the calibrated P-value. In MIMIC IV, question 1 produced a calibrated P-value of 0.894 and BA[F] = 0.875 (95% credible interval 0.385 to 0.992); the apparent one-year mortality reduction of 16.9% was entirely attributable to systematic bias and the association was not usable as effect evidence. Question 2 also failed layer 1, with a calibrated P-value of 0.1026, and BA[F] = 0.460 placed it in the "competitive, no verdict" zone. Conclusions and RelevancePairing the calibrated P-value with BAF and its 95% credible interval turns a binary credibility judgement into a three-channel report (signal existence, effect size, and bias fraction). Despite TARGET-adherent design, doubly robust TMLE, and 12 negative controls, both clinical questions in this study still failed to qualify as effect evidence, with question 1 demonstrating complete bias domination and BAF quantifying the systematic error that remained. The reporting standard proposed here can be applied to any observational study that includes negative controls, without requiring additional data.

papers.title: MID-LIFE LEISURE-TIME PHYSICAL ACTIVITY IS ASSOCIATED WITH LOWER HIP FRACTURE RISK IN UK BIOBANK
papers.abstract: Unstructured AbstractLeisure time physical activity (LTPA) in mid-life may have beneficial effects on risk factors for hip fracture in later life. Conversely, physical activity may increase fracture risk through risk of injury, and the optimal amount of physical activity for reducing hip fracture risk remains unclear. We explored the associations between volume and intensity of LTPA in mid-life, and subsequent risk of hip fracture ascertained from linked health data. This prospective observational study used middle aged adults aged 40-65 years from UK Biobank. LTPA volume (LTPAv) was derived from self-reported walking, moderate and vigorous activity at baseline (2006-2010). Cox proportional hazard and Fine-Gray sub-distribution models were used to estimate the association between activity and hip fracture, which was sex-stratified. From 324,284 participants with complete data 53% were female and mean age at baseline was 54.5 (SD 7.3). Across 16 years of follow-up there were 2,674 hip fractures. In terms of LTPA volume, the lowest risk of hip fracture occurred in quintile 3 for women (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.67-0.91), and men (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.60-0.90), relating to approximately one hour/day of leisure time physical activity. When activity intensities were examined separately, the lowest estimated hazards were observed for vigorous activity, at quintile 4 in women (HR 0.65, 95% CI 0.55-0.76) and quintile 3 in men (HR 0.64, 95% CI 0.52-0.79), corresponding to approximately 60-90 minutes of vigorous activity per week. In conclusion, moderately high volumes of mid-life physical activity, particularly vigorous activity, were related to lower risk of subsequent hip fracture, but these relationships appear to attenuate at higher volumes. Lay SummaryIt is not clear whether being active in mid-life, aged 40-65 years, reduces your risk of having a hip fracture in older age. We used data from 324,284 people from the UK Biobank, a long running health study, to understand this better. We found that people who were more active had a lower risk of hip fracture. Risk was lowest among people doing about an hour a day of leisure-time physical activity overall, but less benefit was observed with higher amounts. When we looked at different activity intensities, those doing about 60-90 minutes a week of more vigorous activities like running had the lowest risk. This suggests that both the amount and intensity of activity matters.

papers.title: Carbonaceous Components Underlying Wildfire Smoke PM2.5-Associated Alzheimer's Disease and Related Dementias in Older US Adults
papers.abstract: Wildfire smoke exposure is increasing across the U.S., but the long-term neurological effects of smoke-specific fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and its carbonaceous components remain uncertain. Using Medicare data from 2002 through 2019, we examined incident Alzheimers disease (AD) and Alzheimers disease and related dementias (ADRD) among 39,678,630 fee-for-service Medicare beneficiaries followed from 2005 through 2019. We identified 3,501,414 incident AD cases over 258.5 million person-years and 8,377,416 incident ADRD cases over 248.6 million person-years. We linked the cohort with annual, high-resolution estimates of smoke and non-smoke PM2.5 mass and carbonaceous components (elemental and organic carbon) and fitted stratified Cox proportional hazards models. Per 1 {micro}g/m3 increase, smoke PM2.5 was associated with incident AD (hazard ratio [HR], 1.015, 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.005-1.026) and ADRD (1.029 [1.024-1.035]). Smoke carbonaceous fraction was also associated with AD (1.063 [1.042-1.085]) and ADRD (1.090 [1.077-1.103]). Within the ADRD endpoint, smoke-related associations exceeded their corresponding non-smoke associations on a per-unit-mass basis. Per interquartile range, associations were smaller for smoke PM2.5 (AD, 1.005 [1.002-1.008]; ADRD, 1.009 [1.008-1.011]) than for non-smoke PM2.5 (AD, 1.086 [1.079-1.094]; ADRD, 1.048 [1.043-1.053]). Associations varied across geographic, racial, socioeconomic, and clinical subgroups. Long-term wildfire smoke exposure, particularly its carbonaceous fraction, was associated with higher incidence of AD and ADRD among older U.S. adults. The associations correspond to 2,284 and 11,142 incident cases per year of AD and ADRD attributable to smoke PM2.5 among older Medicare beneficiaries, with the carbonaceous fraction accounting for most of this burden. These findings support the use of source-resolved and composition-specific smoke metrics in dementia research and wildfire-smoke health-impact assessments.

papers.title: The transition to retirement and dementia risk: An application of sequence analysis
papers.abstract: BackgroundRetirement is a major life transition that may influence cognitive aging. Retirement pathways are becoming increasingly diversified, yet evidence on how heterogeneous retirement trajectories relate to dementia risk remains limited. This study used sequence and cluster analysis to characterize thousands of transition-to-retirement trajectories, including retirement timing and work intensity, to estimate associations with dementia risk. MethodsWe used data from 13,879 participants in the U.S. Health and Retirement Study. Our exposure was transition-to-retirement trajectories between ages 51 and 75 identified using sequence and cluster analysis. Our outcome was a validated algorithmically derived dementia probability measure. We estimated associations between trajectory clusters and dementia risk beginning at age 76 using generalized estimating equations, adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics. Inverse probability weights were used to account for attrition. ResultsWe identified ten distinct transition-to-retirement trajectories characterized by differences in timing of retirement, part-time work, disability, and labor force attachment. Compared with individuals retiring after full-time work in their early-to-mid 60s, dementia risk was similar among those retiring earlier or later from full-time work. In contrast, individuals with sustained part-time employment between ages 51 and 75 had lower odds of dementia (OR: 0.62, 95% CI: 0.48, 0.80), while trajectories characterized by prolonged disability were associated with higher odds of dementia (OR: 1.53, 95% CI: 1.22, 1.91). ConclusionsRetirement timing alone showed limited association with later-life dementia risk, whereas sustained part-time employment and disability-related trajectories were more strongly associated with dementia risk. These findings suggest that employment intensity and health-related exit from the labor force may be more relevant for dementia risk than retirement timing, and that gradual and flexible work-to-retirement transitions may benefit brain health.

papers.title: Associations between commonly consumed beverages and the oral microbiome in three US cohort studies
papers.abstract: Multiple external factors shape human microbial communities. Beverages represent particularly frequent dietary exposures that may impact oral microbiome composition. We examined associations of coffee, tea, alcohol, sugar-sweetened beverages, artificially-sweetened beverages, and fruit juice consumption with the oral microbiome in three large cohort studies (n=5,598). Beverage consumption was assessed by food frequency questionnaire and categorized as non-consumers and tertiles of intake among consumers, except fruit juice, which was categorized into quartiles. DNA from oral wash specimens was sequenced (16S rRNA, V4 region). Associations with alpha and beta diversity and individual genera were assessed using multivariable linear, logistic, count-based regression models and weighted permutation-based models accounting for multiple comparisons in genus-level analyses. Only alcoholic beverage consumption was associated with all alpha diversity metrics; the highest tertile of alcohol drinking was associated with 10.18 (95% CI: 5.56, 14.80) greater observed amplicon sequence variants vs. non-consumers. All beverages accounted for 4.06% of variability in beta diversity (unweighted UniFrac); in univariable models, alcoholic beverages had the largest R{superscript 2} among individual beverages (0.86%) and accounted for the majority (25/28, 89.3%) of genus-level associations, mostly with beer and liquor. For example, high alcoholic beverage intake (T3 vs. non-consumers) was associated with 2.25 and 2.17 times the odds of having Megasphaera and Peptostreptococcus, respectively, and 23% lower abundance of Lautropia. Alcoholic beverage consumption was strongly associated with oral microbes, including taxa linked to poor oral health; these findings suggest that alcohol-associated differences in the oral microbiome may have implications for oral and systemic health.

papers.title: Burden of Non-Communicable Diseases Attributable to Polygenic Risk and Its Association with Healthcare Utilization in Taiwan
papers.abstract: BackgroundNon-communicable diseases (NCDs) impose substantial population burden. Their polygenic architecture informs early risk stratification through polygenic risk scores (PRS). Previous studies reported elevated-PRS burden comparable to some modifiable risk factors (MRFs), yet evidence remains confined to European populations. We quantified the PRS-attributable NCD burden in Taiwan. MethodsLinking Taiwan Biobank and National Health Insurance Research Database (N {approx} 140K), we analyzed 42 high-burden NCDs. Elevated genetic risk (PRSe; top 10%) was assessed using Cox models. We estimated population attributable fractions (PAFs) and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) using Taiwan-specific estimates from Global Burden of Disease 2023, and examined associations between an integrated PRS (iPRS) and healthcare utilization. FindingsStrongest PRSe associations occurred for atrial fibrillation (AFib; HR = 3.56 [95% CI: 3.23-3.92]) and gout (2.41 [2.33-2.49]), yielding PAFs of 20% and 12%, respectively, while population-level attributable DALYs were largest for type 2 diabetes (T2D), intracranial hemorrhage (ICH), and lung cancer. At the individual level, PRSe corresponded to 1.50 [1.42-1.57] healthy life-years lost for T2D and 0.57 [0.40-0.76] for ICH, approaching 2.4 years for the top 1% PRS. Polygenic attributable burden was overall greater in men. For several diseases, PRSe-associated PAF and DALYs exceeded those of individual MRFs (e.g., smoking, alcohol use). Top-decile iPRS was linked to 23.9% (15.0-33.6%) more hospital days, 19.1% (13.2-25.3%) more inpatient visits, and 9.6% (6.9-12.4%) more outpatient visits. InterpretationPolygenic risk accounts for a measurable--and for several diseases, MRF-comparable--share of NCD burden in Taiwan, providing a quantitative foundation for integrating genetic liability into preventive care and health planning. FundingNational Taiwan University Academic Research-Career Development Project, Yushan Young Fellow Program from the Ministry of Education (MoE), and the Population Health Research Center from Featured Areas Research Center Program within the framework of the Higher Education Sprout Project by the MoE in Taiwan.
